sectionTitle: Solar system; stability of orbital motions; satellites (physics only)

specStatements.text: Within our solar system there is one star, the Sun, plus the eight planets and the dwarf planets that orbit around the Sun. Natural satellites, the moons that orbit planets, are also part of the solar system.
Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy.
The Sun was formed from a cloud of dust and gas (nebula) pulled together by gravitational attraction.
Students should be able to explain:
• how, at the start of a star's life cycle, the dust and gas drawn together by gravity causes fusion reactions
• that fusion reactions lead to an equilibrium between the gravitational collapse of a star and the expansion of a star due to fusion energy.
A star goes through a life cycle. The life cycle is determined by the size of the star.
Students should be able to describe the life cycle of a star:
• much more massive than the Sun.
Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements. Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.
The explosion of a massive star (supernova) distributes the elements throughout the universe.
Students should be able to explain how fusion processes lead to the formation of new elements.
Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites (both natural and artificial) to maintain their circular orbits.
Students should be able to describe the similarities and distinctions between the planets, their moons, and artificial satellites.
(HT only) Students should be able to explain qualitatively how:
• (HT only) for circular orbits, the force of gravity can lead to changing velocity but unchanged speed
• (HT only) for a stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes.

concepts.definition: One star, the Sun, together with the eight planets and the dwarf planets that orbit around the Sun. The natural satellites (moons) that orbit those planets are part of the solar system too.
A large body that orbits the Sun. There are eight planets in our solar system. A planet does not produce its own light; it is seen because it reflects light from the Sun.
A body that orbits the Sun but is much smaller than the eight planets. Dwarf planets are part of the solar system; they orbit the Sun in their own right rather than orbiting a planet.
A natural body that orbits a planet rather than orbiting the Sun directly. The Moon is the Earth's natural satellite. Moons are part of the solar system.
A body that releases energy from nuclear fusion in its core, so it emits its own light. Our solar system contains one star, the Sun; everything else in the solar system orbits it.
A galaxy is an enormous collection of stars held together by gravity. The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains our Sun, and our whole solar system is only a small part of it.
A cloud of dust and gas in space. The Sun was formed from such a cloud, and every star begins its life cycle as one.
Every part of a nebula attracts every other part. This gravitational attraction pulls the dust and gas together, so the cloud contracts and becomes denser and hotter at its centre.
The hot, dense object formed as gravity draws the dust and gas of a nebula together. It becomes a star once the temperature is high enough for fusion reactions to begin.

The joining together of light nuclei to form heavier nuclei, releasing energy. In a young star, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium nuclei. Fusion is not burning and it is not the splitting of nuclei.
The long, stable stage of a star's life, during which hydrogen is fused into helium. How long this stage lasts, and what follows it, is determined by the size of the star.

In a stable star the gravitational collapse acting inwards is balanced by the expansion due to fusion energy acting outwards. Because the two effects are equal and opposite, the star stays the same size.
The stage a star about the size of the Sun enters after the main sequence, when it swells to a far larger size and its surface glows red.
The small, very dense, hot remnant left behind when a star the size of the Sun sheds its outer layers at the end of the red giant stage.
What a white dwarf becomes once it has cooled so far that it no longer emits visible light. This is the final stage in the life cycle of a star the size of the Sun.
The stage entered after the main sequence by a star much more massive than the Sun. It expands to an even greater size than a red giant before the star explodes.
The explosion of a massive star at the end of its life. Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova, and the explosion distributes the elements throughout the universe.
The extremely dense remnant left at the centre after a supernova. This is the end point for a massive star that is not massive enough to form a black hole.
The remnant left after the supernova of the most massive stars. Its gravitational field is so strong that not even light can escape from it.

Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements: light nuclei fuse into successively heavier nuclei, up to iron. Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova, whose explosion then spreads all these elements throughout the universe.
The path of one body around another. Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites, both natural and artificial, to maintain their circular orbits.

A man-made object placed in orbit around the Earth or another planet. Like a moon, it is held in its orbit by the gravitational force of the body it orbits; unlike a moon, it was built and launched by people.

concepts.term: Direction of the gravitational force in a circular orbit
concepts.definition: For a body in a circular orbit the gravitational force acts towards the centre of the orbit, at right angles to the direction in which the body is moving.

Velocity is speed in a given direction. Because gravity acts at right angles to the motion in a circular orbit, it continually changes the direction of travel without changing how fast the body is going, so the velocity changes while the speed stays the same.

An orbit in which the speed and the radius are matched, so the body keeps circling at the same distance. For a stable orbit the radius must change if the speed changes: a faster satellite must orbit at a smaller radius, a slower satellite at a larger radius.

misconceptions.question: Are dwarf planets and moons part of the solar system?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The solar system is the Sun plus the eight planets, the dwarf planets and the moons that orbit the planets.
misconceptions.misconception: The solar system is just the Sun and the eight planets; dwarf planets and moons are separate things that happen to be nearby.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Primary-school diagrams and models show only the Sun and eight planets in a neat row, so anything left out of that picture is not counted as belonging.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists the members of the solar system as the Sun, the eight planets, the dwarf planets, and the natural satellites (moons) that orbit planets. All of them orbit within the Sun's gravitational field, so all of them belong.

misconceptions.question: What kind of object is the Sun?
misconceptions.correct: The Sun is a star, and it is the only star in our solar system.
misconceptions.misconception: The Sun is not really a star; it is a huge ball of fire at the centre, and the stars are the small points of light you see at night.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The Sun looks nothing like a night-time star because it is so much closer, and everyday language treats 'sun' and 'star' as different words for different things.
misconceptions.correction: A star is a body that releases energy by nuclear fusion and emits its own light; the Sun does exactly that. The other stars look like faint points only because they are enormously further away.

misconceptions.question: What does a moon such as the Earth's Moon orbit?
misconceptions.correct: A moon orbits a planet. Moons are called natural satellites for that reason.
misconceptions.misconception: Moons orbit the Sun like everything else in the solar system; they just happen to stay near a planet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that the Sun's gravity dominates the solar system, and then apply that single idea to every body without asking which body each one actually circles.
misconceptions.correction: The defining feature of a natural satellite is that it orbits a planet: the Moon circles the Earth, held by the Earth's gravitational force. Planets and dwarf planets orbit the Sun; moons orbit planets.

misconceptions.question: How many planets orbit the Sun?
misconceptions.correct: Eight.
misconceptions.misconception: There are nine planets, because Pluto is one of them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Older books, posters and family memory still list nine planets, and Pluto is often the most memorable name on the list.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the solar system contains eight planets. Pluto is classed as a dwarf planet: it still orbits the Sun and is still part of the solar system, but it is not one of the eight planets.

misconceptions.question: How does our solar system relate to the Milky Way galaxy?
misconceptions.correct: Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy, which contains a vast number of stars.
misconceptions.misconception: The solar system and the Milky Way are the same thing, or the Milky Way is something inside the solar system.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words 'solar system', 'galaxy' and 'universe' are all used loosely to mean 'space', so students never fix the order of scale between them.
misconceptions.correction: Fix the scale: one star (the Sun) with its planets makes our solar system; a huge number of stars makes the Milky Way galaxy; a huge number of galaxies makes the universe. The solar system sits inside the galaxy, not the other way round.

misconceptions.question: Where is the Sun within the Milky Way galaxy?
misconceptions.correct: The Sun is one ordinary star among the enormous number in the galaxy, and the solar system is only a small part of it.
misconceptions.misconception: The Sun must sit at the centre of the Milky Way, because everything orbits the Sun.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that the Sun is at the centre of the solar system and then stretch that fact to the whole galaxy.
misconceptions.correction: The Sun is at the centre of our solar system only. On the scale of the galaxy it is one star among a vast number, and the specification stresses that our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way.

misconceptions.question: What pulled the cloud of dust and gas together to form the Sun?
misconceptions.correct: Gravitational attraction between the parts of the cloud pulled it together.
misconceptions.misconception: Something pushed the cloud together - a shock wave, a collision, or the pressure of the gas squeezing inwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'squashing something up' with pushing, and gravity is usually pictured as a downward pull on Earth rather than a mutual attraction between any masses.
misconceptions.correction: Every mass attracts every other mass. In a nebula this gravitational attraction pulls the dust and gas inwards, so the cloud contracts on its own. The specification names gravitational attraction as the cause.

misconceptions.question: Which comes first, the gravitational collapse of the cloud or the fusion reactions?
misconceptions.correct: Gravity draws the dust and gas together first; the resulting rise in temperature then causes fusion reactions to begin.
misconceptions.misconception: The fusion energy is what draws the cloud together, so the star is already fusing before it collapses.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fusion is the most striking idea in the topic, so students make it the cause of everything rather than a consequence of the collapse.
misconceptions.correction: Follow the order in the specification: dust and gas drawn together by gravity causes fusion reactions. The contraction raises the temperature and density enough for nuclei to fuse; fusion is the result, not the trigger.

misconceptions.question: When do fusion reactions start in a forming star?
misconceptions.correct: Only once gravity has made the protostar dense and hot enough for hydrogen nuclei to fuse.
misconceptions.misconception: Fusion starts as soon as the dust and gas begin to gather, so any clump of gas in space is a star.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see 'gas cloud' and 'star' on the same diagram and treat the change as instant, with no condition attached.
misconceptions.correction: Fusion needs extremely high temperature and density. Gravity supplies these by compressing the material of the protostar; until that threshold is reached there is no fusion, and the object is not yet a star.

misconceptions.question: Is the Sun burning its fuel?
misconceptions.correct: No. The Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion, in which hydrogen nuclei join to form helium nuclei.
misconceptions.misconception: The Sun is a giant fire; it burns hydrogen the way a gas hob burns gas, and one day the fire will go out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language ('burning', 'the Sun's fire') and the visible glow of flames make combustion the obvious model for anything hot and bright.
misconceptions.correction: Burning is a chemical reaction between substances and needs oxygen; it rearranges atoms but leaves nuclei untouched. Fusion is a nuclear change in which nuclei themselves join together, releasing far more energy.

misconceptions.question: What happens to nuclei in a fusion reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Light nuclei join together to form heavier nuclei, releasing energy.
misconceptions.misconception: Fusion is when large nuclei split into smaller ones, releasing energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fission and fusion are met close together, both release energy and both begin with 'f', so the two processes get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Fusion = fuse = join. Fission = split. In a star, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium; that building-up process is also how heavier elements are made, which splitting could never do.

misconceptions.question: Why does a main sequence star stay the same size for so long?
misconceptions.correct: Because the gravitational collapse inwards is balanced by the expansion due to fusion energy outwards - the star is in equilibrium.
misconceptions.misconception: Once fusion starts, gravity stops acting on the star, so there is nothing left to make it collapse.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read 'balanced' as 'one effect has been switched off', instead of two effects that are still there but equal and opposite.
misconceptions.correction: Both effects act at all times. Gravity keeps pulling the star inwards and the energy from fusion keeps pushing it outwards; because they are equal in size the star neither shrinks nor expands. If the fusion energy fell, gravity would immediately make the star contract.

misconceptions.question: What decides which stages a star passes through in its life cycle?
misconceptions.correct: The size of the star.
misconceptions.misconception: It is decided by how hot the star is, what colour it looks, or how old it is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Colour and temperature are the properties students can most easily observe or picture, so they are assumed to be the controlling factor.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: the life cycle is determined by the size of the star. Two stars of very different sizes follow different routes after the main sequence, however hot or old either of them is.

misconceptions.question: What will the Sun become at the end of its life cycle?
misconceptions.correct: A red giant, then a white dwarf, which finally cools to a black dwarf.
misconceptions.misconception: The Sun will explode as a supernova and leave a black hole behind.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Supernovae and black holes dominate films and documentaries, so they become the default ending for any star.
misconceptions.correction: Only stars much more massive than the Sun end in a supernova and leave a neutron star or a black hole. A star the size of the Sun becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf, then a black dwarf.

misconceptions.question: In what order does a star the size of the Sun pass through the red giant and white dwarf stages?
misconceptions.correct: Red giant first, then white dwarf, then black dwarf.
misconceptions.misconception: The star shrinks to a white dwarf and then swells into a red giant at the very end.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume a star must get steadily smaller as it dies, so the biggest stage cannot come after the smallest.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the sequence in order: nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf. The star expands into a red giant when its main sequence stage ends, then sheds its outer layers to leave the hot, dense white dwarf.

misconceptions.question: Do all stars end their lives in a supernova?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only stars much more massive than the Sun explode as a supernova.
misconceptions.misconception: Every star finishes with a supernova; it is just the normal way a star dies.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The supernova is the memorable event in the topic, and students who learn only one ending apply it to every star.
misconceptions.correction: The route a star takes is determined by its size. A star the size of the Sun ends quietly as a white dwarf and then a black dwarf; there is no explosion. A supernova belongs only to the massive route.

misconceptions.question: What is left behind after a supernova?
misconceptions.correct: A neutron star, or a black hole if the original star was massive enough.
misconceptions.misconception: Every supernova leaves a black hole, and a neutron star is just another name for one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both remnants are described as extremely dense, and students who meet them together compress two outcomes into one.
misconceptions.correction: There are two possible outcomes, and which one occurs depends on the mass of the original star. Massive stars leave a neutron star; the most massive of all leave a black hole, from which not even light can escape.

misconceptions.question: Where are elements heavier than iron produced?
misconceptions.correct: In a supernova.
misconceptions.misconception: All the elements, including gold, lead and uranium, are made by ordinary fusion inside a star's core.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn correctly that fusion in stars produces the naturally occurring elements, and then apply it without noticing the limit the specification places on it.
misconceptions.correction: Fusion in stars builds nuclei up as far as iron. Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova, so a star that never explodes never makes them.

misconceptions.question: How did heavy elements come to be part of the Earth?
misconceptions.correct: They were made in stars and in supernovae, and the supernova explosion distributed them throughout the universe before the Earth formed.
misconceptions.misconception: The elements in the Earth were made on Earth, or they have simply always existed everywhere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet elements first in chemistry as fixed, given substances, so nothing prompts them to ask where the atoms themselves came from.
misconceptions.correction: Fusion processes in stars produce all the naturally occurring elements, and the explosion of a massive star distributes those elements throughout the universe. The material the Earth formed from already contained them.

misconceptions.question: Is there a force acting on a satellite orbiting the Earth?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Gravity provides the force that keeps the satellite in its circular orbit.
misconceptions.misconception: There is no gravity in space, which is why satellites and astronauts float instead of falling.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Footage of astronauts floating is read as proof that gravity has vanished, and 'zero gravity' is used as an everyday label for it.
misconceptions.correction: The Earth's gravitational field extends far into space; without it a satellite would travel in a straight line and leave. It is the gravitational force that continually pulls the satellite towards the Earth and so keeps it in orbit.

misconceptions.question: Are the forces on an orbiting satellite balanced?
misconceptions.correct: No. There is a resultant gravitational force on the satellite, directed towards the Earth.
misconceptions.misconception: The satellite stays in orbit because gravity pulling inwards is balanced by an outward force that throws it out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect steady motion to mean balanced forces, and the feeling of being flung outwards on a fairground ride supplies an invented outward force.
misconceptions.correction: Nothing pushes the satellite outwards. The single unbalanced gravitational force acts towards the centre of the orbit and continually changes the satellite's direction; that is precisely what keeps it circling instead of flying off in a straight line.

misconceptions.question: What counts as a satellite?
misconceptions.correct: Any body in orbit around a planet - the Moon is a natural satellite, and a launched spacecraft is an artificial satellite.
misconceptions.misconception: A satellite is by definition man-made, so the Moon is not a satellite.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday use of the word 'satellite' (satellite TV, satellite dish) refers only to technology, so the natural meaning is never met.
misconceptions.correction: Natural and artificial satellites are alike in that both orbit a planet and both are held in orbit by gravity. The distinction is only in origin: moons formed naturally, artificial satellites were built and launched by people.

misconceptions.question: A satellite moves round a circular orbit at a steady speed. Is its velocity constant?
misconceptions.correct: No. Its direction is constantly changing, so its velocity is constantly changing.
misconceptions.misconception: If the speed is not changing then the velocity is not changing either, so nothing is accelerating.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Speed and velocity are used as synonyms in ordinary speech, so the vector nature of velocity is easily forgotten once numbers are involved.
misconceptions.correction: Velocity is speed in a given direction, so a change of direction alone is a change of velocity. In a circular orbit gravity acts at right angles to the motion, turning the satellite without speeding it up.

misconceptions.question: Gravity pulls on an orbiting satellite. Why does the satellite not get faster and faster?
misconceptions.correct: Because in a circular orbit the gravitational force acts at right angles to the direction of motion, so it changes the direction of travel but not the speed.
misconceptions.misconception: A force always makes something speed up, so gravity must be making the satellite go faster all the time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every earlier example of a force acting on a moving object - a falling ball, a car accelerating - has the force along the direction of motion, so students expect the same here.
misconceptions.correction: What a force does depends on its direction relative to the motion. A force along the motion changes speed; a force at right angles to it changes only direction. Gravity on a circular orbit is always at right angles to the motion, pointing to the centre.

misconceptions.question: A satellite in a stable orbit is made to travel faster. Can it stay at the same distance from the Earth?
misconceptions.correct: No. If the speed changes, the radius must change for the orbit to stay stable; a faster satellite orbits at a smaller radius.
misconceptions.misconception: Speeding up just means the satellite completes each lap more quickly around the same circle.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday picture is a car going faster round the same roundabout, where the driver simply steers harder; students do not notice that a satellite cannot choose its inward force.
misconceptions.correction: The gravitational force at a given distance is fixed, and only one speed matches that force. Change the speed and the orbit is no longer stable at that distance: for a stable orbit at a higher speed the radius must be smaller.

misconceptions.question: Can a satellite orbit stably at any radius with any speed?
misconceptions.correct: No. For each radius there is one speed that gives a stable orbit, so speed and radius are linked.
misconceptions.misconception: Any combination will do; a satellite orbits wherever it is put, at whatever speed it happens to have.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams show satellites at several different heights without stating the speed, leaving the impression that the two quantities are independent.
misconceptions.correction: Speed and radius are tied together for a stable orbit: satellites in low orbits must travel faster than those in high orbits. If the speed is wrong for the radius, the orbit is not stable and the radius changes.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly describes what our solar system contains?

options.text: One star and eight planets only; dwarf planets are not included
options.rationale: A student who remembers only the primary-school diagram of the Sun and eight planets excludes everything else.

options.text: One star, eight planets, dwarf planets and their natural satellites
options.rationale: This is exactly the membership the specification gives: the Sun, the eight planets and the dwarf planets that orbit it, plus the moons that orbit planets.

options.text: One star, nine planets and the dwarf planets that orbit them
options.rationale: A student who still counts Pluto among the planets gives nine rather than eight.

options.text: Eight planets and their moons, with the Sun counted as a planet
options.rationale: A student who does not accept that the Sun is a star treats it as one more body in the list.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the moons in our solar system is correct?

options.text: They orbit the Sun, keeping pace with the nearest planet
options.rationale: A student who thinks the Sun's gravity governs every body has moons circling the Sun rather than a planet.

options.text: They orbit planets, but they are not part of the solar system
options.rationale: A student who defines the solar system as the Sun and its planets leaves the moons outside it.

options.text: They orbit the Sun, and each one is classed as a dwarf planet
options.rationale: A student who confuses the two categories of small body treats every moon as a dwarf planet.

options.text: They orbit planets, and they are part of the solar system
options.rationale: Natural satellites are moons that orbit planets, and the specification counts them as part of the solar system.

mcqs.stem: How is our solar system related to the Milky Way galaxy?

options.text: The Milky Way is one of the galaxies inside our solar system
options.rationale: A student who has not fixed the order of scale puts the larger structure inside the smaller one.

options.text: The solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy
options.rationale: The specification states that our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy, which contains a vast number of stars.

options.text: The solar system sits at the exact centre of the Milky Way
options.rationale: A student who knows the Sun is central to the solar system stretches that fact to the whole galaxy.

options.text: The Milky Way and the solar system are two names for one thing
options.rationale: A student who treats 'galaxy' and 'solar system' as loose synonyms for space sees no difference between them.

mcqs.stem: The Sun formed from a cloud of dust and gas called a nebula. What pulled this cloud together?

options.text: The pressure wave from a nearby exploding star pushing it in
options.rationale: A student who thinks squashing must involve a push looks for something external to compress the cloud.

options.text: The gravitational attraction between the parts of the cloud
options.rationale: Every part of the nebula attracts every other part, and this gravitational attraction makes the cloud contract.

options.text: The magnetic attraction between the dust grains in the cloud
options.rationale: A student reaching for an attractive force names the one most often demonstrated in the laboratory.

options.text: The energy released by fusion reactions already taking place
options.rationale: A student who makes fusion the cause of everything has it acting before the cloud has collapsed.

mcqs.stem: As gravity draws the dust and gas of a nebula together, the material becomes denser and hotter. What does this eventually lead to?

options.text: The temperature becomes high enough for fusion reactions to start
options.rationale: The contraction raises the temperature and density until hydrogen nuclei can fuse, which is how a star begins its life cycle.

options.text: The gas begins to burn, releasing energy by chemical reaction
options.rationale: A student who models the Sun as a fire expects hot gas to ignite and burn.

options.text: The largest nuclei split apart, releasing energy by fission
options.rationale: A student who has swapped fission and fusion picks the splitting process as the energy source.

options.text: The cloud cools again as it radiates the energy back to space
options.rationale: A student who knows hot objects lose energy to their surroundings assumes the cloud simply cools down again, missing that gravity keeps compressing it.

mcqs.stem: Which nuclear process releases the energy of a newly formed star?

options.text: Hydrogen nuclei fuse together to form helium nuclei
options.rationale: In a young star, light hydrogen nuclei join to form heavier helium nuclei, releasing energy.

options.text: Large nuclei such as uranium split into smaller nuclei
options.rationale: A student who confuses fusion with fission describes the splitting process met in nuclear reactors.

options.text: Hydrogen gas burns in oxygen to release heat and light
options.rationale: A student using the combustion model supplies an oxidant and calls the process burning.

options.text: Helium nuclei break apart to form hydrogen nuclei
options.rationale: A student who knows hydrogen and helium are involved but has the direction reversed builds light nuclei from heavy ones.

mcqs.stem: A main sequence star such as the Sun stays the same size for billions of years. Why?

options.text: Gravity no longer acts on the star once fusion reactions have started
options.rationale: A student who reads 'balanced' as 'switched off' removes gravity from the picture altogether.

options.text: The expansion caused by fusion is far stronger than the collapse
options.rationale: A student who thinks one effect must win chooses fusion, without noticing that the star would then keep growing.

options.text: Gravity pulling it inwards is balanced by the expansion caused by fusion energy
options.rationale: The star is in equilibrium: gravitational collapse inwards and expansion due to fusion energy outwards are equal and opposite.

options.text: The star has used up its hydrogen, so nothing can change its size
options.rationale: A student who links stability to nothing happening assumes the reactions have stopped, when in fact they are the reason it is stable.

mcqs.stem: Suppose the energy released by fusion in a stable star suddenly fell. What would happen to the size of the star?

options.text: It would expand, because gravity acts outwards from the centre
options.rationale: A student who has the direction of gravity wrong predicts the opposite change.

options.text: It would stay the same, because gravity stops once fusion starts
options.rationale: A student who thinks gravity switched off at the start of the star's life sees nothing left to act.

options.text: It would stay the same, because the star's mass has not changed
options.rationale: A student who links size only to mass overlooks the balance of the two competing effects.

options.text: It would contract, because gravity would then be unbalanced
options.rationale: With less outward expansion from fusion energy, the inward gravitational collapse is no longer balanced, so the star gets smaller.

mcqs.stem: What determines the stages that a star passes through in its life cycle?

options.text: The size of the star when it forms
options.rationale: The specification states that the life cycle of a star is determined by the size of the star.

options.text: The surface temperature of the star
options.rationale: A student who links stellar behaviour to how hot a star is chooses temperature.

options.text: The colour the star appears from Earth
options.rationale: A student who has met red giants and white dwarfs assumes colour is the controlling property, not just a description.

options.text: The age the star has already reached
options.rationale: A student who thinks all stars follow one fixed path treats age as the only variable.

mcqs.stem: A star the size of the Sun comes to the end of its main sequence stage. Which sequence of stages follows?

options.text: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf
options.rationale: A star the size of the Sun swells into a red giant, sheds its outer layers to leave a white dwarf, and finally cools to a black dwarf.

options.text: White dwarf, then red giant, then black dwarf
options.rationale: A student who assumes a dying star only ever shrinks puts the small stage before the large one.

options.text: Red giant, then supernova, then neutron star
options.rationale: A student who thinks every star ends in an explosion applies the massive-star ending here.

options.text: Red super giant, then supernova, then black hole
options.rationale: A student who has only learnt the dramatic route gives the massive-star sequence for the Sun.

mcqs.stem: The Sun will eventually run out of hydrogen in its core. What will it finally become?

options.text: A black hole, formed when its core collapses inwards
options.rationale: A student whose picture of stellar death comes from documentaries gives the most dramatic ending.

options.text: A supernova, which throws its outer layers outwards
options.rationale: A student who believes all stars explode chooses the supernova, which belongs only to massive stars.

options.text: A neutron star, left at the centre of the old star
options.rationale: A student who remembers the remnants but not which route they belong to picks a massive-star outcome.

options.text: A white dwarf, which then cools to form a black dwarf
options.rationale: The Sun is not massive enough to explode; after the red giant stage it leaves a white dwarf that cools into a black dwarf.

mcqs.stem: A star much more massive than the Sun leaves the main sequence. Which sequence of stages follows?

options.text: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf as the star cools
options.rationale: A student who knows only one life cycle gives the Sun's route for a massive star.

options.text: Red super giant, then supernova, then a black hole in every case
options.rationale: A student who has merged the two possible remnants leaves out the neutron star.

options.text: Red super giant, then supernova, then neutron star or black hole
options.rationale: A massive star expands into a red super giant and explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or, if massive enough, a black hole.

options.text: Red super giant, then neutron star, then supernova as it explodes
options.rationale: A student who has the order confused puts the remnant before the explosion that produces it.

mcqs.stem: After a supernova, what decides whether the remnant left behind is a neutron star or a black hole?

options.text: The colour of the supernova flash
options.rationale: A student who thinks colour controls a star's behaviour uses it to decide the outcome.

options.text: The surface temperature of the star
options.rationale: A student who substitutes temperature for size chooses the property that is easier to picture.

options.text: The mass of the star that exploded
options.rationale: The life cycle is determined by the size of the star: only the most massive stars leave a black hole, others leave a neutron star.

options.text: The number of elements produced
options.rationale: A student who has just learnt that supernovae make heavy elements links the remnant to that instead of to mass.

mcqs.stem: Where are the naturally occurring elements heavier than iron produced?

options.text: In the main sequence stage of any large star
options.rationale: A student who knows fusion makes elements applies it without the limit at iron.

options.text: In the core of every star, along with iron
options.rationale: A student who treats all fusion as equivalent has heavy elements made wherever iron is.

options.text: In the hot early Earth, soon after it formed
options.rationale: A student who has never asked where atoms come from assumes the Earth made its own.

options.text: In a supernova, the explosion of a massive star
options.rationale: The specification states that elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.

mcqs.stem: How do fusion processes inside a star lead to the formation of new elements?

options.text: Heavy nuclei split, so lighter elements build up in the core
options.rationale: A student who has swapped fusion and fission describes elements being made by splitting.

options.text: Nuclei join, producing every element up to uranium in the core
options.rationale: A student with the right mechanism but no limit has ordinary fusion making the heaviest elements.

options.text: Nuclei join to make heavier nuclei, building elements up to iron
options.rationale: Fusion joins light nuclei into successively heavier ones, which is how the elements up to iron are made inside a star.

options.text: Atoms react chemically, combining to form new elements
options.rationale: A student using a chemical model changes the substances but not the nuclei, so no new element could form.

mcqs.stem: The Earth contains elements such as gold and lead. How did these elements come to be in the material from which the Earth formed?

options.text: They were formed inside the Earth after it had cooled
options.rationale: A student who has never asked where elements come from assumes they were made where they are found.

options.text: They were made by fusion inside the Sun and blown out
options.rationale: A student who ignores the iron limit has the Sun producing elements far heavier than it can.

options.text: They have existed since the universe began, unchanged
options.rationale: A student who treats elements as fixed, given substances sees no need for them to be produced at all.

options.text: A supernova explosion spread them out across the universe
options.rationale: The explosion of a massive star distributes the elements throughout the universe, so later material already contains them.

mcqs.stem: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around the Earth. What keeps it in that orbit?

options.text: Nothing does; there is no force acting on it out in space
options.rationale: A student who believes there is no gravity in space sees the satellite as simply floating.

options.text: The gravitational force of the Earth acting on the satellite
options.rationale: Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites, natural and artificial, to maintain their circular orbits.

options.text: Balanced forces: gravity inwards and a force outwards
options.rationale: A student who expects steady motion to need balanced forces invents an outward force to cancel gravity.

options.text: The push of its engines, which are kept running all the time
options.rationale: A student who thinks motion needs a driving force assumes the satellite must be powered continuously.

mcqs.stem: What do the Moon and a communications satellite orbiting the Earth have in common?

options.text: Both are kept in orbit by gravity
options.rationale: A natural satellite and an artificial satellite are alike in orbiting a planet, held there by the gravitational force.

options.text: Both were launched into orbit by people
options.rationale: A student who thinks 'satellite' means man-made assumes the Moon was placed there too.

options.text: Both travel in orbit around the Sun
options.rationale: A student who has every body orbiting the Sun misses that both of these orbit the Earth.

options.text: Both formed naturally with the Earth
options.rationale: A student who overcorrects and calls every satellite natural loses the distinction of origin.

mcqs.stem: A satellite travels round a circular orbit at a steady speed. Which statement about its motion is correct?

options.text: Its velocity is constant because its speed is constant
options.rationale: A student who treats speed and velocity as the same quantity sees no change at all.

options.text: Its speed increases because gravity is always pulling on it
options.rationale: A student who expects any force to speed an object up applies that rule to a force at right angles to the motion.

options.text: Its velocity changes because its direction keeps changing
options.rationale: Velocity is speed in a given direction, and gravity acting towards the centre continually changes the direction of travel.

options.text: Its speed and velocity both change as it goes round
options.rationale: A student who senses something is changing assumes the speed must change as well as the direction.

mcqs.stem: A satellite in a stable circular orbit is made to travel at a greater speed. What must happen if the orbit is to stay stable?

options.text: The radius of its orbit can stay the same
options.rationale: A student picturing a car going faster round the same roundabout keeps the radius fixed.

options.text: The radius of its orbit must decrease
options.rationale: For a stable orbit the radius must change if the speed changes; a faster satellite orbits at a smaller radius.

options.text: The radius of its orbit must increase
options.rationale: A student who thinks going faster means being thrown further out reverses the relationship.

options.text: The mass of the satellite must increase
options.rationale: A student who does not link speed to radius looks for some other quantity to adjust instead.
